title: Read(README.md)
detail:
# Neoism

<!-- Sample edit: testing agent file changes without changing visible documentation. -->

**Your terminal. Your IDE. Your agent platform.**

Neoism is a local-first, open-source agentic IDE. A modern terminal, a full code editor, and Neoism's own agent runtime and SDK come together in one persistent workspace.

Run commands, delegate coding tasks, and make changes yourself. Move between shell output, source files, and agent conversations while staying in your project. Build your own agent-powered applications and tools on the same framework that powers the IDE.

**MIT licensed. Native desktop applications for Linux, macOS, and Windows.**

[Download](https://github.com/parkers0405/neoism/releases) · [Get started](docs/README.md) · [Agent SDK](neoism-agent/sdk/typescript/README.md) · [Art](https://neoism.ai/art)

## Build with agents. Stay in control.

- **A command line you can work with.** Ghostty-powered terminals organize commands and output into blocks, with completion previews, command history, filtering, copying, and reusable commands. Choose the block interface or the classic terminal.
- **A full IDE alongside your shell.** Edit with Tree-sitter, Vim motions, multicarets, and language-server completion, diagnostics, navigation, rename, code actions, and formatting. Keep source files, Git changes, and rich Markdown close at hand.
- **Agents that work with your project.** Give agents tasks, follow their progress, inspect tool calls and changes, and respond to permission requests. Choose your model provider and extend their tools through plugins and MCP.
- **An agent framework you can build on.** Neoism includes its own embeddable Rust agent runtime, TypeScript SDK, and plugin framework. Build applications and integrations around sessions, streaming events, tools, permissions, and provider connections.
- **A workspace that stays with you.** Arrange files, terminals, and agents in tabs and splits. Your local workspace daemon keeps shell and agent sessions running independently of the frontend, with remote connections and collaboration available when you need them.

Looking for a **Warp alternative**? Neoism combines a block-based terminal with a full IDE and a built-in agent development platform, in a local-first, MIT-licensed application.

Your application, workspace services, and agent runtime run locally by default. Model inference happens with your configured provider; connected providers, MCP servers, and remote workspaces have their own data boundaries. See [what local-first means](docs/README.md#local-first-by-default).

## Install

Download a native bundle from [Releases](https://github.com/parkers0405/neoism/releases). Release targets are Linux x86_64, macOS Apple Silicon, and Windows x86_64.

| Platform | Installation |
|---|---|
| Linux x86_64 | Extract `neoism-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`, then run `./neoism` from the extracted directory. To install into `~/.local/bin`, run `bash install-bundle.sh . "$HOME/.local"` there. |
| macOS Apple Silicon | Open the `neoism-darwin-aarch64.dmg` disk image and drag `Neoism.app` into Applications. |
| Windows x86_64 | Run `Neoism-x86_64.msi`. A portable `neoism-windows-x86_64.zip` is also available. |

Keep the complete extracted bundle together: executables, native libraries, runtime resources, and licenses are required. The bundle's `web/app` and `web/native` directories contain resources for the native desktop application. See the [packaging notes](neoism-frontend/gpuix/README.md#run) for distribution details.

### Nightly and updates

Nightly builds for all three platforms are published as prereleases on the [Releases page](https://github.com/parkers0405/neoism/releases). Choose the latest nightly there for a fresh installation, or update an installed copy:

```sh
neoism update --nightly
```

Use `neoism update` for the stable channel. Windows updates use the MSI installer. Linux upgrades retain the previous installed bundle while its windows or daemons are running; a later upgrade prunes it after those processes exit.

## Make something

Open your project, press Alt+T for a terminal, and run your first command. Alt+E opens files, Alt+A starts an Agent conversation, Ctrl+P opens Finder, Alt+P opens commands, and Ctrl+S saves your work.

Open **Documentation** from the command palette, or run `neoism docs`, for the local handbook and Scalar API reference. The same documentation is [available online](https://neoism.ai/api/docs/). New Notes vaults start with one root-level `Welcome.md` checklist covering the basics; the full handbook stays out of your notes.

Start with [documentation access](docs/README.md), explore the [block terminal](docs/terminal.md), or build with the [Agent SDK](neoism-agent/sdk/typescript/README.md). The [frontend reference](neoism-frontend/gpuix/README.md) covers detailed behavior, shortcuts, and current limitations.

## Software is art, too

**Art should be free to enjoy. Software should be, too.**

You can explore Michelangelo's *The Last Judgment / Christ the Judge detail* in [Neoism Art](https://neoism.ai/art). The gallery offers a public-domain reproduction to look closely at, learn from, and enjoy. We bring that same spirit to the tools we build.

Software is a creative work. You should be able to use it, understand how it works, change it, and share what you make. Neoism is free and open source under the [MIT license](LICENSE): the freedom to make the workspace your own is part of the product.

## Configuration and connections

Configuration is JSONC in `~/.config/neoism/config.json`, or under `NEOISM_CONFIG_HOME`. Launch options include `--workspace ID`, `--config PATH`, `--theme NAME`, `--font-size SIZE`, and `--maximized`.

A normal launch reuses the local workspace daemon or starts one when needed. To attach to another host, use `neoism --daemon ws://HOST:7878/session`; explicit endpoints never start a local daemon. The daemon owns PTYs, files, language servers, Git, search, collaboration, and Agent sessions.

## Build and develop

The root Makefile provides the local Linux workflow. Install Node.js/npm, a C/C++ toolchain, pkg-config, Fontconfig/FreeType, GBM, xkbcommon, Wayland/X11 development libraries, and the Vulkan loader. Scripts install project-local Bun and fetch the pinned Blaze, GPUIX, and Ghostty toolchains as needed.

Clone with `git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/parkers0405/neoism.git`, or initialize the pinned shared docs in an existing checkout with `make docs-init`. `make docs` builds the local handbook and API site without compiling the application. Documentation source is maintained in [neoism-docs](https://github.com/parkers0405/neoism-docs), shared with the website through pinned Git submodules.

```sh
make build                       # build services and the native bundle
./neoism-frontend/gpuix/dist/neoism
make run                         # build services/core, then run from source
make dev                         # source frontend with hot replacement
make check                       # types, design, Rust, and dependency checks
make test                        # workspace, bridge, and frontend tests
```

For a Linux source installation, `./install.sh` builds and installs into `~/.local/lib/neoism-gpuix/bin`, leaving `~/.local/bin/neoism` and existing desktop shortcuts untouched. Launch it with `~/.local/lib/neoism-gpuix/bin/neoism`. To install at the usual user prefix instead, use `./install.sh --prefix "$HOME/.local"`; this replaces that launcher's bundle.

Local Makefile builds and tests use `scripts/blaze.sh`; the native bridge defaults to Blaze but supports an explicitly selected Cargo build. Published release CI uses Cargo for both services and the bridge on Linux, macOS, and Windows through [`scripts/build-gpuix-release.mjs`](scripts/build-gpuix-release.mjs), with platform packaging in [`release-neoism.yml`](.github/workflows/release-neoism.yml). These are distinct workflows, not automatic compiler fallbacks. The [frontend guide](neoism-frontend/gpuix/README.md#run) documents bridge selection, build profiles, native-window checks, and performance measurement.

Nix users can run a built Linux bundle with `nix run .#neoism-runtime -- /path/to/neoism`. The Nix source package provides daemon/Agent services; build the desktop bundle through `make build`. Building those services with Blaze uses `nix build .#neoism-services --option sandbox relaxed` and requires a trusted Nix user; `nix develop` runs the pinned compiler outside that filesystem sandbox.

## Architecture and extensions

The native frontend combines SolidJS with GPUIX/GPUI rendering, shared Rust editor engines, and Ghostty terminal emulation. Workspace services and the embeddable agent runtime live behind the desktop interface.

| Path | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| [`neoism-frontend/gpuix`](neoism-frontend/gpuix/README.md) | Native GPUIX application, window, input, composition, and Ghostty adapter |
| `neoism-frontend/shared` | Shared editor, Markdown, panel state, layout, interaction, and paint interfaces |
| `neoism-paint` | CPU fonts, shaping, glyph rasters, image data, and retained document layout |
| `neoism-workspace-daemon` | Workspace services, PTYs, transport, persistence, and collaboration |
| [`neoism-agent`](neoism-agent/README.md) | Embeddable agent runtime, server launcher, plugins, SDK, and tools |
| `neoism-backend` | Shared persistent configuration and server registry |

Build on the [TypeScript SDK](neoism-agent/sdk/typescript/README.md), extend the runtime with [native/process Agent plugins](docs/plugins.md), or connect tools through MCP. See the [Agent API reference](docs/agent-plugins.md) and [Agent runtime guide](neoism-agent/README.md) for contracts, permissions, and deployment options.

Neoism is MIT-licensed; see [LICENSE](LICENSE) and [NOTICE](NOTICE) for licensing and third-party acknowledgements.

(End of file - total 107 lines)

detail:
# Changelog

All notable user-facing changes to Neoism are documented here.

## [0.7.142] - 2026-10-26

### Chat readiness, index recovery, and browser control

- Memoizes provider readiness per catalog generation and prefetches bounded display-only history previews to reduce prompt admission and chat-opening work.
- Promotes queued prompts immediately when stopping a run, with queue snapshot reconciliation and admission regression coverage.
- Uses the indexed session-list sidecar for child-session queries, omits server-only context bookkeeping from roster responses, and repairs a corrupt derived FTS registry before retrying affected writes once.
- Refines native browser observation/actions and includes Neoism Browser Control source, Chrome/Firefox extensions, build scripts, tests, and dependency notices. The separate Node runtime is disabled initially and must be built/staged separately; these files are not automatically bundled in desktop release packages.
- Extends frame-spike diagnostics and render scheduling refinements.

This release includes the complete working-tree source batch. Browser extension/runtime checks are distinct from live browser automation validation; no live browser session or cross-platform runtime behavior is claimed solely from source inclusion. Existing database upgrade and rollback cautions from 0.7.140 still apply.

## [0.7.141] - 2026-10-26

### Agent pane scrolling and cancellable discovery

- Clips quad geometry before rasterization while retaining full-quad UV coordinates, avoiding repeated full-card shading for occlusion fragments. User-measured live apply_patch diff-card scrolling improved from 117 to 144 FPS, with GPU busy falling from 69% to 39%; these are workload-specific measurements, not universal guarantees.
- Stages and premeasures older-history pages within a per-frame budget before prepending, removing user-measured 30-60 ms upward-scroll hitches.
- Replaces quadratic inline wrapping with running-width tracking and exact measurement near the wrap edge.
- Compiles Tree-sitter highlight grammars and decodes agent image attachments off the native render thread.
- Extends opt-in `NEOISM_FRAME_SPIKE_LOG=1` diagnostics with main-thread handler time between frames.
- Makes MCP discovery and provider-catalog preparation cancellable, scopes tool lookup to the requested service, and adds cancellation/queued-prompt regression coverage.

Includes all modified and untracked files present at release staging, including concurrent-session changes and local memory files, as explicitly requested. The user reports 13 shared-UI tests, 12 desktop agent tests, and one hanging `subagent_runtime_snapshot` test fail identically on the preceding HEAD; those baseline issues are not claimed fixed or passing here.

## [0.7.140] - 2026-10-25

### Official Turso upgrade and history I/O

- Upgrades to the official crates.io Turso 0.8.3 release, pinned exactly, with matching application and transport-contract lockfiles.
- Replaces whole-session enumeration with indexed child-session queries, handles parent cycles, and limits permission/question authorization to sessions with pending requests while failing closed on unreadable sessions.
- Skips unchanged native FTS projections with revision and race guards, and migrates the derived search index transactionally on first upgraded startup.
- Losslessly compresses eligible journal payloads using a versioned, checksummed envelope and resumable bounded background migration; bounds replay by rows and stored/decoded bytes without truncating history at short pages.
- Recovers durable child-completion notifications after parent initialization failures without duplicate user turns, and closes streams on decode/replay failures rather than silently presenting empty history.
- Adds codec, replay, authorization, family-query, completion-recovery, and isolated old-format FTS migration fixtures, plus an optional development-derived activation profile.

- Preserves provider/model-scoped OpenAI Responses replay and reasoning phases across tool continuations; enables batch patch editing by default with explicit opt-out.
- Adds slim history projections, targeted exact-glob file search, deduplicated nearby project instructions, faster streaming Markdown layout, persistent copy selection, and immediate idle-compaction feedback.
- Retains seven days of event-journal replay by default (`NEOISM_AGENT_EVENT_RETENTION_DAYS=0` disables pruning), with durable sequence high-water marks and explicit replay-expired notifications. Canonical conversation history is preserved.
- Adds manual offline `neoism-agent db compact` and opt-in frame timing diagnostics. Stop all database users and make an independent backup before manual compaction: its retained copy is post-pruning, active-user detection is best-effort, and the file swap is not guaranteed failure-atomic.

**Upgrade and rollback:** preserve a consistent pre-upgrade database backup. New and migrated compressed event records cannot be replayed by older TEXT-only backends, so a binary-only downgrade is unsafe. The first upgraded startup rebuilds the derived FTS index synchronously and can take longer for large indexes. Online journal retention reuses pages rather than shrinking the file; physical shrinking requires explicit offline maintenance.

## [0.7.139] - 2026-10-25

### Agent streaming, readiness, and experimental UI foundations

- Reduces repeated agent catalog/database reads and conversation-search index work, preserving scope-valid provider readiness during background refreshes.
- Streams incremental tool-input deltas across native, web, and SDK reducers instead of repeatedly cloning growing snapshots.
- Bounds retained live events and queued WebSocket reply bytes, closing lagging streams for client reconciliation, and spools external-agent output to managed files with bounded previews.
- Loads prompt context from the latest completed compaction boundary while preserving persisted conversation history.
- Adds experimental NeoUI layout, input, component, and Settings foundations behind an opt-in feature; stable packages retain the existing Settings UI.
- Optimizes development-profile code and dependencies without changing the release profile.

This stable release includes the merged `feature/neoui` work. Event and reply limits reduce memory amplification but do not impose a global daemon heap or output-disk bound. Servo and CEF runtimes remain excluded from production packages.

## [0.7.138] - 2026-10-24

### Model discovery and scaled text correction

- Includes the model discovery, offline picker recovery, rendering caches, question navigation, and license packaging changes prepared for 0.7.137.
- Fixes scaled canvas text sampling outside its glyph allocation on CPU, Vulkan, WGSL, and Metal, preventing stale or neighboring atlas pixels from contaminating glyph edges.
- Adds grayscale/RGBA contaminated-padding fixtures and strengthens font invalidation coverage with live-raster and final-pixel comparisons.

The 0.7.137 production run was canceled before publication after its renderer regression test failed. Its tag remains unchanged; this release carries the correction and is published only after the complete platform matrix passes. No live GPU or affected-machine Windows runtime validation is claimed.

## [0.7.137] - 2026-10-24

### Model discovery and text rendering

- Expands bundled model metadata and refreshes discovery in the background with bounded retries, preserving successful in-memory results when disk-cache writes fail.
- Updates open model pickers as discovery completes without losing search or selection; keeps useful offline options, bounds hydration waits, and isolates account-authoritative Codex models from API-key and other-account catalogs.
- Adds bounded, collision-checked text shaping and font-aware measurement caches, retained caret geometry, cached diff measurements, horizontal token seeking, and offscreen diff-card culling.
- Highlights the latest question in the navigation rail at the live bottom edge.
- Includes regression fixtures, model catalog provenance, and distributed license notices.

This is a stable production release, available through plain `neoism update` after all platform builds and packaging checks pass. Continuous animations and the existing Servo/CEF worker exclusions are preserved. Slow-network Windows behavior still requires affected-machine runtime verification.

## [0.7.136] - 2026-10-23

### Chat hydration, provider readiness, and frame responsiveness

- Improves chat opening with incremental/cached history, bounded ingestion work, background generated-image hydration, and shared attachment payloads.
- Adds bundled offline provider/model metadata and makes optional discovery nonblocking for connection UI. Keeps warm account-scoped readiness metadata through bounded refresh failures while preserving per-model Codex maxima and effective input budgets.
- Adds capability-verified machine-wide Agent target selection, generation-scoped remote catalogs, explicit activation settings, and reconnect handling without automatic prompt replay.
- Adds a question navigation rail and refines image-preview/modal behavior, composer wrapping/layout, and account-selection reconciliation.
- Presents previous-good terminal frames during lock contention instead of blocking unrelated UI; moves Git/notes work off the critical path and improves cached diagnostic and bounded LRU bookkeeping.
- Defers Vulkan texture retirement until acquired-slot fence reuse and uses GPU-ordered atlas uploads rather than ordinary-path idle/cross-slot CPU waits, preserving teardown synchronization.

This is a stable production release, available through plain `neoism update` after all platform builds and packaging checks pass. Visible continuous animations remain enabled. Existing first-terminal behavior, scoped authorization, trusted-user hosting limits, and Servo/CEF worker exclusions are preserved.

## [0.7.135] - 2026-10-23

### Pull requests, systems management, and Agent presentation

- Adds GitHub pull-request discovery, creation/opening, immutable comparison tabs, Changes/Conversation/Checks views, review drafts, comments/approvals/change requests, thread replies/resolution, and viewer-side browser links.
- Adds a repository-scoped paginated PR inbox with search, labels, state/sort filters, relationship grouping, responsive detail layout, and retained drafts.
- Adds explicit current-workspace or managed-worktree checkout with repository/snapshot verification and authoritative document checks; dirty or collaborative documents refuse unsafe transitions. Checkout is not an untrusted-repository sandbox.
- Adds muted, noninteractive PR loading skeletons while retaining meaningful errors/empty states. PR detail headers and tabs scroll away so Code/Timeline can use the full detail viewport, with clipped input routing and review-sheet scroll ownership.
- Adds native Systems management for saved SSH recipes and connection lifecycle, cancellation/generation guards, shared tunnels, and palette navigation. Browser clients report desktop-only management.
- Refines the floating composer, inset tray, wrapping, snapped seams, silhouette-aware painting/hit regions, timeline scrollbar, and browser drag ownership. Adds deferred inverse clipping while preserving preceding render output and atlas/UV metadata.
- Improves provider readiness caching, history-operation serialization, and undo deletion/search cleanup. Uses proportional Geist for PR presentation and updates provider artwork with attribution notices.
- Includes PR documentation and the intentional removal of the source-only typesafe-AI skill files.

This is a stable production release, available through plain `neoism update` after the full platform matrix passes. Servo and CEF workers remain separate experimental components and are not packaged.

## [0.7.134] - 2026-10-22

### Git review, editor lifecycle, and LSP navigation

- Adds native/shared/browser Git review tabs, canonical inline editing, projected source/carets, precise block stage/discard, full-file baselines, commit review, source navigation, and toolbar/gutter/layout improvements.
- Preserves canonical document ownership through review/close/save transitions and reconciles CRDT restores against remembered baselines. Exact block actions reject stale or unsupported selections instead of falling back to whole-file mutation.
- Serializes daemon Git operations asynchronously with bounded admission and scope-aware protocol handling. Browser Git refresh follow-ups retain their captured workspace and reject retired-context replies.
- Improves rich LSP hover presentation with bundled Geist prose, selection/copy and safe links, declaration/type-definition navigation, negotiated capabilities, asynchronous discovery/caching, and exact-position queries.
- Improves Agent catalog/conversation caching, credential/scope invalidation, initial-history previews, preload reconciliation, loading presentation, and activity handling.
- Refines finder behavior, tab/focus/scroll interactions, overlay occlusion, Git review geometry, and first-terminal measured startup layout. Includes the Geist font and its license attribution.

This is a stable production release, available through plain `neoism update` after platform builds and packaging checks pass. Existing first-terminal directory following, trusted-user hosting limits, and Servo/CEF worker exclusions are preserved.

## [0.7.133] - 2026-10-20

### Windows startup, provider connection, and search scheduling

- Preserves the initial optimistic prompt through Windows session hydration/binding, fences pre-admission idle snapshots, and corrects queue ownership/busy projections. Aligns Windows daemon signing-key location with desktop/Agent conventions.
- Adds provider-connection progress, browser fallback, explicit retry, cancellation and late-result suppression, secret clearing, transport-failure settlement, and account/model reconciliation across native/shared hosts.
- Correlates catalog requests and failures across the protocol, daemon, WASM, and browser. Both HTTP failure paths now terminate their correlated request while retaining legacy uncorrelated forms.
- Improves conversation-search eligibility lookup, ancestry reuse, bounded cursor work, and batched payload hydration without dropping canonical authorization. Removes the fixed two-second search deadline while retaining admission and work caps; idle index optimization runs off-thread.
- Bounds native navigator fetch concurrency and pending-query replacement, with debounce, stale-generation rejection, and interruptible retry.
- Uses shared branded provider callback pages with escaped failure text and accurate authorization-received wording rather than claiming an unverified connection.

This is a stable production release, available through plain `neoism update` after the platform matrix passes. Existing first-terminal behavior, trusted-user hosting boundaries, and Servo/CEF worker exclusions are preserved.

## [0.7.132] - 2026-10-19

### Agent startup, request handling, and queue recovery

- Improves cold-start readiness waits and health validation while moving optional Tailscale discovery off the local-startup critical path.
- Uses pooled desktop HTTP clients on a dedicated runtime, bounded responses, request deadlines, and HTTP message framing rather than waiting for connection closure. SSE retains separate polling/cancellation behavior.
- Moves native prompt admission and session preference/interaction writes off the UI thread, captures request ownership at submission, and preserves uncertain-delivery state for reconciliation and explicit retry instead of blindly replaying writes.
- Improves durable queue admission and run handoff, startup cancellation recovery, retained-prompt execution rollover, and dequeue-before-provider-output ordering.
- Carries directory scope through native/browser conversation search, batches canonical authorization hydration, and classifies expected busy/budget errors without false 500 responses. Improves bounded sidebar history preloads and catalog reconciliation.
- Preserves streamed assistant text when a late empty snapshot arrives without an explicit retry reset; explicit retries still clear their previous baseline once, and nonempty corrections keep their existing merge behavior.
- Includes the committed Windows candidate/fixture MSI checkpoint and standalone validation recovery workflow, allowing future saved-package validation retries without recompiling. This does not establish the cause of previous runner losses.

Readiness and request deadlines are separate budgets, not a single end-to-end latency promise. Agent structured errors and daemon proxy responses have different envelopes; uncertain mutations require reconciliation. This is a stable production release, available through plain `neoism update` after the platform matrix passes. Existing first-terminal behavior, trusted-user hosting boundaries, and browser-worker exclusions are preserved.

## [0.7.131] - 2026-10-19

### Background preparation, framing, and startup presentation

- Adds configurable wallpaper blur, centered aspect-preserving cover/optional contain fitting, normalized positioning, platform overrides, and Settings/Lua/documentation integration. Pathless framing can adjust an inherited pack wallpaper without replacing its opacity.
- Prepares native startup wallpaper decode/blur on a background worker with request coalescing, generation checks, source-aware cache keys, validated cache contents, bounded image dimensions, and optional-cache fallback. GPU upload remains on the render thread; picker/pack transaction paths can still prepare images synchronously.
- Coordinates initial window reveal with successful presentation and background preparation, including completion wakeups, returned-error/cleared-image fallthrough, and X11 hidden-window redraw handling.
- Improves configuration round trips for color arrays/null and named margin sides so Lua patches preserve nonempty serialized appearance settings.
- Preserves existing terminal initialization and browser-worker exclusions. First-frame presentation is platform-sensitive; permanently stalled background preparation is not currently governed by a reveal timeout.

This is a stable production release, available through plain `neoism update` after all platform builds and packaging checks pass. Servo and CEF workers remain separate experimental components and are not packaged.

## [0.7.130] - 2026-10-18

### Production Agent GUI contract alignment

- Aligns the production Agent GUI's runtime/activity snapshot fixtures and consumers with the generated catalog-family contract, including `familyRevision` and required per-session activity maps.
- Carries all search, manual-compaction queue, prompt-cache, presence, evaluation-source, and Nix improvements prepared for v0.7.129. That release did not publish because the production GUI check failed; no feature work is omitted from this patch.
- Validates the production GUI build and tests in addition to the SDK/core, native, WASM, and API contract checks.

This is a stable production release. The failed v0.7.129 tag is not moved or reused; v0.7.130 becomes available through plain `neoism update` after all platform checks pass.

## [0.7.129] - 2026-10-18

### Search, compaction queues, presence, and provider caching

- Adds durable manual-compaction queue controls, serialized admission/cancellation, restart and transfer persistence, and consistent desktop/shared status reconciliation.
- Adds conversation full-text search backed by a durable Turso projection, bounded indexing/backfill, scoped ranking and filters, snippets, and navigator loading/error states across desktop and browser hosts.
- Improves Codex OAuth prompt-cache affinity with account/tenant/workspace/connection scoping and matching request header/body cache keys, while preserving non-Codex behavior and explicit overrides.
- Adds optional client-OS presence metadata through the protocol, daemon, browser publisher, and shared/native rendering while retaining legacy message compatibility.
- Improves subagent activity retention, cached-session/sidebar state, pagination, queue/abort presentation, emphasized links, and input wrapping.
- Includes evaluation-lab source, synthetic suites, and public HARD-51 setup/adapters/locks/tests. Paid/public experiment validation remains separate; generated downloads, environments, and run transcripts are not included. Local asset provenance may require preparation on another machine.
- Includes the committed Nix release-runtime, launcher, source-packaging, shader-tooling, and build/test selection fixes.

This is a stable production release, available through plain `neoism update` after the full platform matrix passes. Existing first-terminal directory following, trusted-user hosting boundaries, contributor credit, and Servo/CEF worker exclusion are preserved.

## [0.7.128] - 2026-10-17

### Conversation navigation and Windows validation hardening

- Adds measured Back / Prev / Next navigation for child conversations, following visible nested-roster order without wrapping and falling back to the authoritative main conversation when a trusted roster is unavailable.
- Shares navigation behavior across native and browser hosts, with clipped, occlusion-aware hit regions, live target revalidation, and stale-geometry clearing on session changes and resets.
- Preserves unsent composer drafts alongside cached conversation state and keeps empty child conversations navigable before their first message arrives.
- Uploads Windows installer/native-test evidence checkpoints before MSI smoke tests, adds timestamped phase/process logging, passes the expected version explicitly, and bounds redirected-output draining and process cleanup waits.
- Retains strict installer checks and reboot suppression. This hardening improves failure bounds and diagnosis; it does not establish that the previous hosted-runner disconnection cause is fixed. Alternate validation workflows do not yet include every release-path safeguard.

This is a stable production release, available through plain `neoism update` after the full platform matrix passes. Existing first-terminal directory following, trusted-user hosting limits, and Servo/CEF worker exclusion are preserved.

## [0.7.127] - 2026-10-16

### MCP authorization, subagent navigation, and rendering

- Adds inline cancellable MCP browser authorization with scope-preserving callbacks, explicit connection retry, and status that distinguishes authorization from an established runtime connection. Coalesces visible catalog refreshes and invalidates stale runtime status.
- Adds bounded MCP presentation metadata and inline raster icons, bundled service artwork, and consistent presentation through tool results, history, and remote timelines. Includes artwork/font provenance and license notices.
- Adds selectable connected-subagent catalog rows with exact child identity and owning-project navigation; parent foreground activity no longer mirrors child execution incorrectly.
- Improves dialog wrapping, clickable links, picker actions, icon cropping, settings layout/navigation, and cursor affordances.
- Adds self-contained branded invite/OAuth handoff pages with embedded Geist font and replayable wordmark animation. Adds analytic antialiased ring rendering across CPU, WebGPU, Vulkan, and Metal backends.
- Improves browser conversation-family handling and hover ownership. Uses measured terminal dimensions for initial PTY creation instead of the placeholder size.

This is a stable production release, available through plain `neoism update` after all platform builds and packaging checks pass. Existing first-terminal directory following, trusted-user hosting boundaries, and Servo/CEF worker exclusion are preserved.

## [0.7.126] - 2026-10-15

### Project conversations, hosting, and native interaction

- Promotes the nightly project-grouped conversation sidebar, global pins, independent pagination, conversation search/navigation, unified directory/image browser, and host-scoped recents to stable.
- Adds bounded Rust tool composition with native/MCP dispatch, schema validation, permissions, cancellation, and visible child-call traces.
- Adds Fast Host invites/deep links, unified server controls, recovery/leave workflows, and persistent-host readiness checks. Improves hosted-family authorization, revocation restoration, namespace continuity, and ordinary/Fast transport contracts.

## [0.7.61] - 2026-08-27

### Fixed

- Fixed watched sessions freezing while the activity pill kept moving.
Three mechanisms were closed: transcript snapshots no longer run on the
SSE reader thread (a slow store read was stalling token delivery for
its whole duration), the scoped event stream caches foreign-session
verdicts instead of walking storage per event, and a lagged event
subscriber is disconnected for clean reconnect recovery instead of
continuing with a hole in its timeline. Two client-side watchdogs
remain as safety nets: a dead-socket detector and a stalled-stream
force-resubscribe with full reconciliation.
- Fixed joined workspaces failing with daemon-credential errors after a
token rotation: every place a daemon token is signed or compared (the
websocket handshake, the agent proxy, credential minting, and agent
verification) now treats the on-disk token as the live trust root with
the startup environment as fallback.

### SDK and API

- Every message part now has a typed schema in the OpenAPI contract:
discriminated part union, status-discriminated tool states, and typed
step-finish token usage and cost. Part events carry the typed part.
- Live events carry a wire-monotone sequence (durable rows persist the
same value), fixing SDK event streams that previously dropped every
event after the first; the SDK dedupes by event id and its event
subscription yields the typed union.
- Added a runnable headless embedding example and handbook coverage for
embedding, hosted multi-tenant authentication, and API stability.

## [0.7.60] - 2026-08-27

### Fixed

- A watched agent session no longer freezes after a provider-overload
retry. The event-stream reader now detects a dead connection (45
seconds without server keep-alives), reconnects, and reconciles the
transcript — live token streaming resumes without closing and
reopening the session.
- Retried responses no longer double their text: the retry's message
reset is honored so re-streamed tokens replace the failed partial
reply instead of appending to it. Late empty snapshots outside a
retry still never regress streamed text.
- Failed release build legs now save their compile caches, so release
retries start warm.

## [0.7.59] - 2026-08-27

This release ships the Agent V2 replatform: the agent server is now a
plugin-first platform with one versioned API, one ordered event bus, a
third-party plugin runtime, and a typed TypeScript SDK.

### Agent V2 platform

- Rebuilt the agent server around internal plugins: providers, tools, agents,
MCP, LSP, PTY, VCS, workflows, semantic search, configuration, and the
system prompt all load as plugins in immutable per-workspace generations
that reload live when configuration changes.
- Every route is served through `/v2/` and described by a committed OpenAPI
document; a parity test keeps plugin-dispatched routes and the spec in
lockstep.
- Replaced the split live/durable event channels with one ordered event bus:
snapshots and deltas broadcast synchronously in publish order, ending
freeze-then-double-stream artifacts and out-of-order thinking cards during
live streams.
- Restored real-time token streaming cadence end to end.
- The session coordinator is the sole in-memory authority on run ownership;
plugin session access is descriptor-validated.
- Plugin generations retire only after active leases release, so in-flight
requests never race a configuration reload.
- The Agent supervisor starts with the workspace daemon, and persisted Agent
settings project into V2 configuration.

### Third-party plugins

- Added the serve-plugin runtime: long-lived `neoism-plugin/2` processes that
register tools, hooks, and event subscriptions over newline-delimited JSON
stdio.
- Plugins load from a command, a local entry file, or an npm package; npm
installs happen in the background and the generation rebuilds live when the
install completes.
- A failing plugin degrades with a visible reason instead of failing the
workspace.
- Added the `@neoism/plugin` authoring package (`definePlugin`/`runPlugin`)
with an SDK client wired to the host server.
- Windows resolves npm and batch shims through `cmd /C` with PATHEXT-aware
executable resolution.

### SDK and typed events

- Typed the V2 event stream: all 34 published event types form a
discriminated union in the OpenAPI document, exhaustively tested against
the server's event vocabulary.
- The TypeScript SDK yields that typed union from its event subscription,
with automatic reconnect and a sequence cursor that deduplicates replays.
- Session, message, artifact, permission, question, provider, catalog, and
plugin operations are all exposed through the generated typed client.
- Added a version-locked npm publish pipeline for the SDK packages.
- The desktop and shared frontends now consume `neoism-agent-core` types
directly for event classification and turn assembly.
- Added TLS to the desktop agent transport for `https://` servers.

### Transcript search

- Session search in the agent side panel now searches full transcripts, not
just titles: matching excerpt chunks render under each session,
word-wrapped to the panel width.
- Every occurrence of the search terms highlights inside the excerpts.
- Semantic ranking blends in when an embeddings provider is configured;
keyword search works without one.
- Multi-word searches fall back to per-term matches when no single message
contains every word.

### Fixed

- New agent responses no longer inherit the previous response's execution
timer: quiescence settles at queue-worker exit, exempts the admitting
prompt's own worker, and reconciles leaked `running` run rows that
silently blocked executions from ever finishing.
- Manual compaction durably finishes its run record instead of leaking a
permanently running row.
- Transcript search no longer fails when plugin routes deliver numeric query
parameters as strings.
- Subagent activity status, timing, and live token streaming stabilized;
live agent timelines stay chronological and reasoning order survives
metadata arrival.
- Notes vault tests no longer race process-global state.

### Documentation

- Documented the V2 platform in the bundled handbook: new Server and API,
Plugins, and SDK pages, an architecture overview, and refreshed Configure,
Tools, and MCP pages.
- GitHub releases now carry these notes automatically from the changelog.

## [0.7.55] - 2026-08-24

### Added

- Added scheduled agent workflows loaded from project or global `workflow/` and
`workflows/` directories.
- Added one-time, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, and interval schedules with
local or IANA timezones, DST handling, month-end clamping, and missed-run
coalescing.
- Added workflow activation, pausing, manual runs, previews, diagnostics,

- Added workflow API routes and OpenAPI definitions for listing, inspecting,
activating, pausing, running, previewing, and reading history.

patterns. Interactive permission requests are denied instead of blocking a
scheduled run indefinitely.
- Added a bundled Scheduled Workflows guide and linked it from the Neoism Agent
documentation.
- Added a rectangular presence-avatar rendering primitive for future shared

### Changed

- Redesigned the agent side-panel usage display as a compact System 7-style
context meter.
- Token totals in the side panel now use the mode indicator's rainbow scramble
transition when their values change.
- Clicking the side-panel usage meter now opens the complete input, output,
cache, reasoning, cost, and model breakdown on desktop and web.

configuration changes, and shut down when disabled or removed.

### Fixed

- Made subagent completion delivery durable and exactly once per logical child
execution using generation identities, stable message IDs, and serialized
child and parent reconciliation.
- Prevented duplicate or quadruple subagent completion notifications from
wrapper, queue-idle, abort, restart, and concurrent sibling races.
- Prevented queued follow-ups from publishing stale wrapper results; one final
completion is emitted after the queued drain finishes.
- Delayed completion acknowledgement until the runtime notification is durably
appended to parent history, while keeping crash recovery idempotent.
- Repaired legacy and malformed persisted subagent completion metadata without
panicking the agent server or duplicating notifications.
- Prevented late permission request and reply cleanup from resurrecting a
finished subagent in the sidebar. Genuine task continuations still reactivate
the child normally.
- Fixed streaming conversation teleports while reading above the bottom by
replacing ambiguous message-ID anchors with stable source and content
identities.
- Fixed timeline anchoring across duplicate or empty IDs, optimistic-to-durable
ID transitions, grouped rows, history prepends, tail appends, row removal,
and active wheel motion.
- Assigned optimistic user prompts their outbound message IDs before display
and reconciled identical prompt text one-to-one.
- Made scheduled-run claiming and schedule-cursor advancement atomic for SQLite
and Turso, preventing a crash from repeating a scheduled occurrence and its
possible side effects.
- Added bounded MCP process shutdown and exact failed-runtime invalidation.

### Tests

- Added and expanded coverage for workflow parsing, validation, recurrence,
timezones, DST, permissions, execution directories, hot reload, atomic run
claims, and restart recovery.
- Added concurrency and recovery coverage for immediate, repeated, and
exactly-once subagent completion delivery.
- Added desktop and shared regressions for permission terminal locks, optimistic

# Neoism Documentation and Frame Scheduling Report

## 1. Scope and Method

This read-only report examines Neoism’s product description, documented release history, and a focused portion of its GPUix frontend frame architecture. The investigation read `README.md` and all 677 lines of `CHANGELOG.md`, searched for the literal lowercase string `frame` under `neoism-frontend/gpuix/src`, and read three matching source files completely.

| Source | Length | Role in this report |
|---|---:|---|
| `README.md` | 107 lines | Product positioning, architecture, installation, development |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | 677 lines | Release evolution, performance claims, validation boundaries |
| `animation/frame-scheduler.ts` | 36 lines | Per-owner scheduling and cancellation |
| `animation/display-clock.ts` | 101 lines | Native display integration and callback batching |
| `agent/AgentTimelineView.tsx` | 280 lines | Conversation rendering, interaction, engine lifetime |

Source paths in the final three rows are relative to `neoism-frontend/gpuix/src`.

The search returned a first page containing 100 matches across 11 files, with additional results available. This was sufficient to select a coherent implementation chain: an animation scheduler, its native presentation adapter, and a substantial consumer. It was not an exhaustive inventory of every frame-related implementation.

No files were modified. No builds, tests, benchmarks, or live rendering experiments were run. Accordingly, conclusions distinguish directly observed source behavior from documented claims and unverified runtime properties.

## 2. Product Model and Architectural Context

The README presents Neoism as a local-first, open-source agentic IDE combining terminals, code editing, and an agent runtime within one persistent workspace. Its central promise is continuity: users should move between shell output, source files, Git changes, and agent conversations without leaving their project context.

The persistence boundary is important. According to `README.md:69`, the daemon owns PTYs, files, language servers, Git, search, collaboration, and agent sessions. The frontend is therefore not the sole owner of ongoing work. Closing or replacing a presentation surface need not imply terminating the underlying activity.

The architecture table places the inspected code within a broader division of responsibilities:

| Component | Documented responsibility | Relevance to frames |
|---|---|---|
| GPUix frontend | Native application, windows, input, composition, Ghostty adapter | Coordinates presentation and user interaction |
| Shared frontend | Editor, Markdown, panels, layout, interaction, paint interfaces | Supplies reusable application behavior |
| `neoism-paint` | Fonts, shaping, rasters, images, retained layout | Provides rendering inputs and retained document data |
| Workspace daemon | Services, PTYs, transport, persistence, collaboration | Supplies asynchronous state changes |
| Agent runtime | Runtime, launcher, plugins, SDK, tools | Produces conversation activity and tool events |

The README explicitly describes SolidJS combined with GPUIX/GPUI rendering and shared Rust editor engines (`README.md:94`). This explains the inspected implementation: reactive TypeScript components coordinate native-core operations rather than implementing the entire conversation renderer as ordinary DOM content.

“Local-first” is also qualified. Model inference uses the configured provider, while MCP servers and remote workspaces introduce separate data boundaries (`README.md:25`). Local ownership should not be interpreted as a guarantee that every connected operation remains on-device.

## 3. Release History: Responsiveness as an Ongoing Concern

The changelog shows sustained work on responsiveness rather than one isolated optimization. Recent entries address rendering cost, event-loop scheduling, background preparation, history ingestion, text measurement, GPU synchronization, and diagnostics.

| Release | Documented change | Performance layer |
|---|---|---|
| `0.7.119-nightly.20261007.1` | Correct overdue redraw handling; reuse wrapping and measurements | Scheduling and CPU work |
| `0.7.131` | Background wallpaper preparation and coordinated window reveal | Startup presentation |
| `0.7.136` | Previous-good terminal frames during lock contention | Contention isolation |
| `0.7.137` | Bounded shaping caches and offscreen diff-card culling | Text and viewport work |
| `0.7.141` | Clip quad geometry; budget history premeasurement | Rasterization and ingestion |
| `0.7.142` | Extend frame-spike diagnostics and scheduling refinements | Observability and pacing |

This progression supports a useful architectural interpretation: visible smoothness depends on controlling work throughout the pipeline, not merely requesting redraws more frequently.

The strongest numerical claim appears in `CHANGELOG.md:21`: user-measured diff-card scrolling improved from 117 to 144 FPS, while GPU busy decreased from 69% to 39%. The changelog appropriately labels those measurements workload-specific. They do not establish universal application throughput.

Similarly, an earlier entry explicitly states that sustained 144 Hz had not been established through an end-to-end before-and-after benchmark (`CHANGELOG.md:387`). These qualifications matter because the inspected scheduler contains a nominal 240 Hz interval, which could otherwise be mistaken for a measured performance guarantee.

The changelog also records unresolved baseline tests and separates source inclusion from live browser validation. Its overall evidentiary style is cautious: packaging, compilation, regression coverage, and affected-machine runtime verification are treated as different claims.

## 4. Per-Owner Scheduling

`frame-scheduler.ts` provides a small scheduling abstraction. Its default interval is:

```ts
export const ANIMATION_FRAME_MS = 1000 / 240;
```

This is approximately 4.17 milliseconds. However, the constant does not independently establish display cadence. The module can delegate to an installed presentation scheduler, and that native-backed path treats ordinary animation requests differently from timer deadlines.

The delay calculation accounts for work already performed:

```ts
export function animationDelay(
  startedAt: number,
  intervalMs: number,
  now = performance.now()
) {
  return Math.max(0, intervalMs - Math.max(0, now - startedAt));
}
```

*Excerpt reformatted from `frame-scheduler.ts:5–7`.*

If preparing the current update already consumed the target interval, the remaining delay becomes zero. The calculation also prevents a negative elapsed duration from increasing the intended wait unexpectedly.

Each `AnimationFrameScheduler` holds at most one pending request. Its `request` method returns immediately when disposed or already pending (`frame-scheduler.ts:27–32`). Consequently, repeated invalidations coalesce instead of creating an accumulating timer queue.

| Operation | Observed behavior |
|---|---|
| `request` | Schedules only when no request is pending |
| Callback execution | Clears pending state before invoking owner code |
| `cancel` | Invokes cancellation and clears pending state |
| `dispose` | Permanently rejects future requests and cancels existing work |

Clearing pending state before invoking the callback permits an animation to request its next step from inside the current step.

One subtle consequence is that duplicate requests do not replace the pending callback. This abstraction is therefore best understood as an invalidation coalescer, not a latest-task queue. Consumers should update shared pending state and let the scheduled callback read it, a pattern visible in the timeline’s pointer handling.

## 5. Native Display Coordination

`display-clock.ts` connects the generic scheduler to renderer-provided frame wakeups. Its narrow renderer interface exposes optional callback registration and wake-request functions. If either capability is absent, installation returns an inactive clock (`display-clock.ts:15–18`).

The adapter separates three scheduling intentions:

| Kind | Handling under the display clock |
|---|---|
| `frame` | Enqueue for a native display opportunity |
| `deadline` | Wait through a timer, then enqueue |
| `yield-frame` | Yield through a zero-delay timer, then enqueue |

This distinction resolves the apparent conflict between the 240 Hz constant and native refresh behavior. Ordinary animation work follows native display opportunities rather than enforcing a JavaScript-generated 240 Hz clock.

The deadline branch also preserves input fairness:

```ts
if (kind === "deadline" || kind === "yield-frame") {
  timer = setTimeout(
    enqueue,
    kind === "yield-frame" ? 0 : Math.max(0, delay)
  );
  delayed.add(timer);
}
else enqueue();
```

*Excerpt reformatted from `display-clock.ts:54–59`.*

Even an overdue deadline yields through the timer path. The source comment explains the concern: immediately feeding overdue work through the native wake queue can starve input when frame preparation exceeds its budget.

Wake requests themselves are deferred through two nested microtasks (`display-clock.ts:40–44`). The documented purpose is to allow Solid mutations and glyph uploads to reach the native UI queue before requesting presentation.

This is an ordering strategy, not proof that all rendering work finishes within a particular deadline. Its actual effectiveness depends on native integration and workload behavior beyond these files.

## 6. Batching, Lookahead, and Idle Behavior

When a native wake arrives, the adapter snapshots queued callbacks, clears the queue, optionally reserves another wake, executes owner updates, and invokes the original renderer callback.

The shared update boundary is concise:

```ts
export function runFrameBatch(
  callbacks: readonly (() => void)[],
  onError: (error: unknown) => void
) {
  batch(() => {
    for (const frame of callbacks) {
      try { frame(); }
      catch (error) { onError(error); }
    }
  });
}
```

*Excerpt reformatted from `display-clock.ts:99–101`.*

Wrapping all owners in one Solid batch lets dependent computations flush after those owners have advanced together. This avoids treating every animation owner as an independent presentation transaction.

Lookahead is enabled unless explicitly disabled. Before preparing a nonempty callback batch, the adapter reserves the next native opportunity (`display-clock.ts:77–82`). Comments explain that registering only after reactive and native mutation flushing can miss the next opportunity.

The reservation is bounded: the final empty wake neither advances owners nor requests another wake. Therefore, the intended steady state after animations settle is parked rather than perpetually polling.

Error behavior deserves qualification. Owner exceptions are passed to `onError`; whether later callbacks continue depends on whether that handler returns. The default handler throws. Native wake rejection clears queued callbacks and reports an error, so this path should not be described as guaranteed delivery.

## 7. Conversation Frames as Application Transactions

`AgentTimelineView.tsx` demonstrates how the infrastructure serves a real application surface. A timeline frame contains more than drawing commands. It can include prepared canvas data, animation state, pointer and selection state, navigation regions, clipboard content, links, outgoing messages, and structured control state (`AgentTimelineView.tsx:24–25`).

The `apply` function updates reactive presentation state in a batch, then handles requested side effects (`AgentTimelineView.tsx:147–163`). This creates a native-to-host boundary: the native engine returns both visual output and actions for the frontend to perform.

| Returned field | Frontend response |
|---|---|
| `commands`, `canvas` | Update paint inputs |
| `pointer`, `selecting` | Update cursor and selection capture |
| `send` | Forward agent messages unless provisional |
| `copy` | Write clipboard content |
| `navigate` | Invoke conversation navigation |
| `animating` | Request another scheduled update |

Link handling distinguishes supported external schemes from file-like targets. Image previews accept a base64 image-data form before passing decoded bytes to the preview callback.

These are presentation integration observations, not a comprehensive security assessment. The implementations of URL opening, file opening, native-core dispatch, and structured controls were not inspected.

## 8. Input Coalescing and Immediate Transitions

The timeline deliberately defers frequent input work. Pointer movement stores the latest local position in `pointerPending`; scheduled frame preparation flushes that position to native core. Wheel events update native scroll state with `deferFrame: true`, then request presentation.

The common scheduling point is:

```ts
const schedule = () => {
  if (!disposed && !engine.lifetime.closed)
    animation.request(() => {
      if (!disposed && bounds.width > 0) call("frame");
    }, startedAt);
};
```

*Excerpt reformatted from `AgentTimelineView.tsx:195–196`.*

This supports coalescing multiple events into scheduled updates. However, “one paint per display frame” should not be interpreted as an unconditional invariant across every path.

Some operations call native core immediately: pointer presses and releases, layout changes, restored positions, and selected-conversation transitions. The source explicitly prioritizes selecting the correct conversation during mounting so a previously viewed child’s frame is not exposed (`AgentTimelineView.tsx:183–186`).

The resulting policy is pragmatic: defer high-frequency motion, but allow immediate correctness-sensitive transitions.

## 9. Retention, Ownership, and Cleanup

Timeline engines outlive individual component mounts. A model-scoped weak map stores engines under serialized workspace/root-conversation keys. This preserves cached layout and scroll state across tab switches while separating workspace ownership.

The nominal cache limit is eight engines. It is not a hard universal bound: pruning skips engines with attached dirty listeners, so active views can keep the map above that target (`AgentTimelineView.tsx:34–43`).

Inactive eviction saves native scroll position before disposal. Restoration requires a matching selected session, avoiding blindly applying one family member’s position to another.

Cleanup exists at several levels:

| Lifetime | Cleanup responsibility |
|---|---|
| Component | Remove dirty listener; dispose scheduler |
| Native view lifetime | Detach subscriptions; release native engine |
| Engine image ownership | Dispose retained image collections |
| Workspace closure | Dispose matching workspace engines |
| Model disposal | Remove subscriptions and clear maps |

Raster retention is associated with the exact engine and renderer. Each `RecentCanvasImages` collection is constructed with a 16 MiB argument, although the collection’s implementation was outside this review. That value should not be presented as a proven application-wide memory cap.

## 10. Conclusions and Verification Boundaries

The inspected architecture consistently separates three concerns: requesting animation work, coordinating native presentation opportunities, and producing conversation-specific frames. Its central techniques are coalescing, batching, explicit ownership, retained engines, deferred frequent input, and bounded lookahead.

The documentation aligns with that design. Recent releases describe reducing work and blocking throughout the rendering pipeline while preserving visible animation. They also avoid equating a local benchmark, packaged source, or passing build with universal runtime correctness.

The most important qualifications are equally clear. The 240 Hz constant is not a demonstrated frame rate. The eight-engine target is soft for active views. Immediate rendering paths coexist with scheduled ones. Error-handler policy affects callback continuation, and native backend behavior remains outside this source sample.

A future runtime investigation could measure input-to-presentation latency, missed display opportunities, idle wake behavior, and active-engine retention. This report establishes the source-level model only. All requested inspection was completed without changing the workspace.
